per_question.question: What are the general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid, a person is generally eligible for **CAP/DA services** if they:

1. **Are enrolled in NC Medicaid**, and their eligibility category does not restrict this service;  
2. **Meet the general Medicaid coverage standards** for the service; and  
3. **Meet CAP/DA-specific waiver criteria**, including nursing-facility level of care and the ability to live safely in the community with supports.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), effective Sept. 1, 2025, §§ 2.1.1, 3.1, 3.2.1)

## General eligibility criteria

### 1) Basic Medicaid eligibility
The beneficiary must be **enrolled in the NC Medicaid Program**. The policy also notes that a beneficiary may have **service restrictions tied to their eligibility category** that make them ineligible for CAP/DA.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 2.1.1, effective Sept. 1, 2025)

### 2) General covered-service criteria
CAP/DA services must meet NC Medicaid’s general coverage standards. The service must be:

- **Individualized, specific, and consistent** with the person’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and not more than the person needs;
- Able to be **safely furnished**;
- Not replaceable by an **equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment** available statewide; and
- Not provided mainly for the **convenience** of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.1, effective Sept. 1, 2025)

### 3) CAP/DA-specific criteria
Medicaid covers CAP/DA when the beneficiary meets the following specific criteria:

- **Meets the required HCBS nursing facility level of care**, as determined by NC Medicaid, and needs long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution, tied to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need;
- A completed **CAP assessment** shows a reasonable indication the person will need at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within **30 calendar days** of evaluation;
- Has a **signed service plan** authorizing one or more waiver services on a monthly basis to help prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management;
- Or has a signed service plan authorizing short-term **equipment, modification, or technology** needed to return to or remain in the primary private residence and prevent institutional placement;
- Is **able to maintain health, safety, and well-being** in the primary private residence or another approved location with formal and informal supports;
- Has paid care needs that can be maintained **within the average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver;
- Has a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate medical services; and
- Has an **emergency back-up and disaster plan** for situations when usual caregivers or staff are unavailable.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.2.1, effective Sept. 1, 2025)

## Scope context
The policy’s case-management entity requirements refer to experience serving **adults 18 years of age and older** with medical complexities or physical disabilities. That supports the adult-focused scope of CAP/DA, though the core eligibility rules above are the direct governing criteria.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 6.4.1, effective Sept. 1, 2025)

## Bottom line
In practical terms, a person generally qualifies for CAP/DA if they are a **current NC Medicaid beneficiary**, **meet medical-necessity and coverage standards**, **meet nursing-facility level of care**, **need CAP/DA waiver services to avoid institutionalization**, can be **safely served in the community**, and have the required **service planning, physician coordination, and backup supports** in place.  
([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), effective Sept. 1, 2025, §§ 2.1.1, 3.1, 3.2.1)

If you want, I can also break this down into a **plain-language client checklist** or explain **what documentation is usually needed to show CAP/DA eligibility**.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health services, the policy does state **continued service** and **discharge** criteria. I could **not verify a separate, expressly labeled “entrance criteria” section** from the text retrieved here, although the policy requires providers to document entrance criteria in the clinical record. The current policy is **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, effective April 15, 2025**. [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Continued service criteria
A beneficiary meets continued service criteria if:

- **Any one** of the following is true:
  - The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
  - The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
  - There is a **tenuous nature of the functional gains**;

**and**

- **Any one** of the following additional criteria is true:
  - The beneficiary has achieved current treatment plan goals, but **additional goals are indicated** by documented symptoms; or
  - The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress** toward meeting goals and documentation supports that.  
  [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) § 3.2.1.2

## Discharge criteria
A beneficiary may be discharged when **any one** of the following applies:

- The beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wishes to receive services**; or
- The beneficiary, based on presentation and lack of improvement despite treatment plan modifications, **needs a more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality** consistent with North Carolina community practice standards.  
  [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) § 3.2.1.3

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For beneficiaries **under age 21**, the **EPSDT special provision can expand coverage for outpatient therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition**. But **EPSDT does not waive prior approval requirements**: if the therapy service requires prior approval, the child’s age does **not** eliminate that requirement. Also, services still cannot be covered if they are **unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, not medical in nature, or not generally recognized as accepted medical practice**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 2.2.1; b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements]

## Effect on outpatient therapy coverage under EPSDT

In Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, outpatient specialized therapies for children are governed by the usual medical-necessity rules, but EPSDT creates an **exception to policy limitations** for Medicaid beneficiaries under 21. The policy text ties this to **42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r)** and makes clear that EPSDT does **not** authorize services that are unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, not medical in nature, or not generally accepted medical treatment. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 2.2.1]

For speech-language and audiology therapy specifically, the policy includes pediatric criteria and visit guidelines for beneficiaries under 21, including ranges based on severity and authorization periods not exceeding six calendar months. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3; § 3.2.1.4; § 5.4]

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

The policy’s ordering-practitioner section applies to outpatient specialized therapies and lists the practitioners who may order services. Those are:

- **Medical Doctor (MD)**
- **Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)**
- **Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)**
- **Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)**
- **Physician Assistant (PA)**
- **Nurse Practitioner (NP)**

[[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.1.2]

## Bottom line

For a Medicaid beneficiary under 21:

- **EPSDT may allow coverage beyond normal policy limits** if the outpatient therapy is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate the child’s condition. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 2.2.1]
- **Prior approval still applies when the service requires it**; EPSDT does not remove that requirement. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements]
- The order must come from an authorized ordering practitioner listed in the policy: **MD, DO, DPM, CNM, PA, or NP**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.1.2]

I checked amendments for Policy 10A and the document returned as authoritative is **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, effective 2025-02-01**.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services for a beneficiary living in an assisted living–type setting, but only under the congregate-setting PCS policy and only if the beneficiary meets that policy’s eligibility criteria.

NC Medicaid’s congregate PCS policy applies to beneficiaries who reside in a North Carolina-licensed Adult Care Home, combination home, or certain licensed group homes. The policy section on covered criteria says the beneficiary must reside in one of those congregate settings and meet functional/medical criteria for PCS. An assisted living facility would need to fit within one of those licensed congregate categories for coverage under this policy. See § 3.2.1 of [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment) (current authoritative document; no amendments returned in the corpus).

The same policy also shows PCS is assessed and delivered in the beneficiary’s congregate facility, which confirms this policy is specifically designed for facility-based PCS rather than only in-home PCS. See § 5.4.3 of [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

Important limits:
- Coverage is not automatic just because the person lives in assisted living.
- The beneficiary must meet the ADL/unmet-need criteria and the other conditions listed in § 3.2.1.
- PCS is not covered if the beneficiary does not meet the policy’s Section 3 criteria. See § 4.1 of [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).
- PCS also is not covered in certain additional situations, including if it is provided somewhere other than the beneficiary’s primary congregate living setting. See § 4.2.1 of [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

So the short answer is: yes, NC Medicaid does cover PCS for some beneficiaries in assisted living/facility settings, if the facility is a qualifying licensed congregate setting and the beneficiary meets the medical and functional eligibility rules.

per_question.question: Can a CAP/DA beneficiary transfer between service providers, and what rules govern transfers of eligible beneficiaries?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. Under the current **CAP/DA policy, a beneficiary can transfer**, and **the Case Management Entity (CME) must coordinate the transfer to prevent gaps in services**. The governing rule is **Section 3.3, “Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries,”** in **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2**. The document returned as the authoritative current version has an effective date of **September 1, 2025**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Governing rule: transfers are allowed, with required coordination

For CAP/DA, transfers of eligible beneficiaries are expressly addressed in **Section 3.3**. That section says the **CME shall coordinate the transfer to prevent gaps in service provisions** and requires these steps **before the transfer**:

- determine the anticipated start date of service;
- coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;
- discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- initiate transfer of the electronic health record in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) to the receiving county;
- arrange a home visit by the receiving entity within **five business days** after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence to assess the environment for health and welfare concerns and plan mitigation and safety; and
- coordinate services to begin on the **first date of the transfer**.  
  **Citation:** 3K-2, § 3.3, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Rule for transfers of eligible beneficiaries to a different county

Section 3.3 gives more specific rules when a **CAP/DA beneficiary is transferring to a different county**:

- the transferring CME and receiving CME coordinate the transfer on the agreed date, or within **less than 30 calendar days of the request to transfer**;
- both agencies discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- the electronic health record is transferred to the receiving county;
- the receiving CME arranges a home visit within **five business days** of the move to the new primary residence; and
- services must start on the **first date of the transfer into the receiving county**.  
  **Citation:** 3K-2, § 3.3, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Supporting context: beneficiary choice of providers

The transfer rule is supported by the person-centered service plan requirements in **Section 5.4.2**, which require the CME to:

- document the authorized provider name, amount, frequency, and duration of each service; and
- ensure the beneficiary’s **right to choose among providers**, evidenced by a signed **Freedom of Choice** form.  
  **Citation:** 3K-2, § 5.4.2, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

That means the policy not only permits coordinated transfers, but also embeds **provider choice** in the service-planning process.

## Implementation detail

Providers participating in CAP/DA must use the **CAP Business System (e-CAP)** and must **accept, decline, or acknowledge service authorizations within three business days** of submission in e-CAP. That helps explain how transfers and reassignments are operationalized, though the transfer rule itself is still in **§ 3.3**.  
**Citation:** 3K-2, § 6.5, [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

A CAP/DA beneficiary **may transfer between service providers/arrangements**, and **§ 3.3 governs transfers of eligible beneficiaries**. The key requirements are coordinated transfer planning by the CME, no gap in services, transfer of records in e-CAP, a timely home visit after a move, and service start on the first date of transfer. Provider choice is reinforced by **§ 5.4.2**.

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. Under HCWD, North Carolina policy says there is **not a maximum total countable income limit for eligibility**, but there **is** a cap on **unearned income** and there are **cost-sharing requirements** as income rises. The surfaced policy states HCWD covers individuals “**regardless of total countable income**,” except for a **150% FPL cap on unearned income**. [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)] [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

## Income limit rule

To qualify for HCWD, a person must “**meet the income requirements for his coverage group**,” and the HCWD policy’s income section says:

- “**Those who have unearned incomes greater than 150% of FPL are not eligible for HCWD.**”
- It also states the policy removed “**limits on countable income except for the 150% of Federal Poverty Level (FPL) cap on unearned income**.” [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)] [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

So, **there is no maximum earned-income / total countable-income ceiling stated in the surfaced HCWD eligibility text**. Instead, higher countable income triggers fees and premiums. The policy also includes the note: “**Refer to Job Aid: Forced Eligibility to process HCWD premium.**” [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

## Premiums and enrollment fee

The policy says:

- If **total countable income is at or below 150% FPL**: **no cost sharing** other than applicable copayments.
- If **total countable income is greater than 150% FPL**: **$50 annual enrollment fee**.
- If **total countable monthly income exceeds 200% FPL**: **monthly premium** is due **in addition to** the $50 annual enrollment fee.
- Premiums increase by income range, and when income **exceeds 450% FPL**, the person must pay a **full premium**. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)] [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC’s CAP/DA waiver rests on the federal **home- and community-based services waiver authority in section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**, as implemented in **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**. In the federal regulations governing waiver requests, CMS requires the state’s application to include the waiver assurances, supporting documentation, and—if applicable—requested waivers of certain Medicaid state plan rules such as statewide application, comparability, and medically needy income/resource rules. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301.

## Federal authority

For the CAP/DA program specifically, the relevant federal authority is the **1915(c) HCBS waiver framework** reflected in **42 CFR § 441.301** and **§ 441.303**. Section 441.301 describes what must be in a waiver request, and it expressly references possible waivers of:
- **section 1902(a)(1)** of the Act (statewide application),
- **section 1902(a)(10)(B)** (comparability of services), and
- **section 1902(a)(10)(C)(i)(III)** (certain income/resource rules for medically needy individuals living in the community), when applicable. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301(a)(2).

## What the state must demonstrate in its waiver application

Under **42 CFR § 441.301**, the state’s application must show, at minimum, that:

- it includes the **assurances required by § 441.302** and the **supporting documentation required by § 441.303**;
- services will be provided under a **written person-centered service plan** approved by the Medicaid agency;
- waiver services will be furnished only to people who are **not inpatients** of a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID;
- beneficiaries served are individuals whom the state determines would, **without waiver services, require an institutional level of care** in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID, as applicable;
- the application identifies who is qualified to develop the **plan of care/person-centered service plan**;
- the application describes the **target group** to be served;
- the application separately defines each **waiver service**; and
- the waiver is limited to one or more permissible **target groups**, including “aged or disabled, or both,” which is the category most relevant to CAP/DA. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301(b).

Section 441.301 also requires the application to address the **person-centered planning process** and the **person-centered service plan**, including informed choice, conflict-of-interest protections, and the individual’s role in directing planning. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301(c).

Under **42 CFR § 441.303**, the state must provide supporting documentation sufficient to back up those assurances, including:

- **health and welfare safeguards** for beneficiaries;
- the **records and information** the state will maintain for **financial accountability**;
- the state’s plan for **evaluation and reevaluation** of beneficiaries, including:
  - who performs the evaluations,
  - how they are done,
  - the evaluation form used,
  - how the state ensures written documentation is maintained, and
  - how reevaluations occur at regular intervals;
- how the state will inform eligible beneficiaries of **feasible alternatives** and allow them to choose between institutional care and HCBS;
- how the state will apply the rules on **post-eligibility treatment of income and resources** for certain beneficiaries; and
- documentation showing **cost neutrality**—that average per-capita Medicaid expenditures under the waiver will not exceed what Medicaid would have spent without the waiver. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.303(a)-(f).

Section 441.303 also requires the state to specify the **number of unduplicated beneficiaries** it intends to serve each year; that number becomes the waiver’s enrollment cap unless CMS approves an increase by amendment. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.303(f)(6).

## NC implementation context for CAP/DA

North Carolina’s CAP/DA clinical policy is the current state implementation document in the corpus, effective **September 1, 2025**. It reflects the state’s operation of the waiver and identifies CAP/DA as a home- and community-based waiver program with three participation options:
- provider-led,
- consumer-led, and
- coordinated caregiving. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

The NC policy also reflects the federal level-of-care and individualized-service concepts by requiring that covered services be individualized, consistent with the beneficiary’s needs, safely furnished, and not more than necessary. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.1.

## Bottom line

The federal authority for NC’s CAP/DA waiver is **Social Security Act § 1915(c)**, implemented through **42 CFR Part 441, especially §§ 441.301 and 441.303**. In its waiver application, North Carolina must demonstrate that the waiver:
- serves an allowable target group,
- limits services to people who meet the required **institutional level of care** absent HCBS,
- uses **person-centered planning** and service plans,
- clearly defines waiver services and provider/planner qualifications,
- protects beneficiary **health and welfare**,
- maintains financial accountability,
- provides beneficiary **choice** between institutional and community services, and
- is **cost-neutral** to Medicaid.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** from a nursing facility bed, subject to specific limits and documentation requirements. No more than **15 consecutive therapeutic leave days** may be taken **without NC Medicaid approval**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8, effective 2024-08-07]

## Conditions that must be met

Therapeutic leave must meet all of these conditions:

- It must be **for therapeutic purposes only**.
- It must be **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**.
- The **necessity for the leave must be documented in the resident’s plan of care**.
- A **therapeutic justification for each instance of leave must be entered in the resident’s health record**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Other important limits

- The nursing facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during the therapeutic leave.
- The facility may not receive any other Medicaid revenue for that resident during the absence besides the bed reimbursement.
- The facility is **not reimbursed for therapeutic leave days that exceed the legal limit**.
- The therapeutic justification is **subject to State review**.
- Facilities must keep a **cumulative record** of therapeutic leave days for each resident, note therapeutic leave status on the **midnight census**, and bill approved leave days as **regular residence days**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## When therapeutic leave does not apply

Therapeutic leave is **not available** when the resident is away **to receive inpatient or nursing services paid for by Medicaid**, whether:
- at another location, or
- at a different level of care in the same facility. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Bottom line

**60 days per calendar year**, with:
- **physician order**,
- **therapeutic purpose**,
- **plan-of-care documentation**,
- **case-specific justification in the health record**, and
- **NC Medicaid approval if more than 15 consecutive days** are needed. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
A PDN provider that ends services must notify **NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, and what they must send depends on why services ended.

## Required notice when the PDN provider terminates services

Under **Section 5.2.4.1, “Notification of Termination,”** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**, which the amendment record returned as the authoritative current document:

- **If the PDN service provider discharges the beneficiary:**  
  the provider **must submit the DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form) to NC Medicaid within five (5) business days**.

- **If the provider discharges the beneficiary because there is another source of nursing coverage:**  
  the provider must **notify NC Medicaid and submit the DMA-3513 within five (5) business days**.  
  That notice must include:
  - **the last date PDN services were provided and can be billed to Medicaid**, and
  - **the name of the other source of coverage**.

- **If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary:**  
  the PDN provider must give NC Medicaid, **within five (5) business days**:
  - **the physician’s order terminating PDN services**, and
  - **the DMA-3513**.  
  The policy also says that **the decision of the attending physician and/or the PDN provider to discharge the beneficiary cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid**.  
  Citation: **3G-1, § 5.2.4.1** in [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment).

## If services stop for Medicaid eligibility or a long interruption

The same section says:

- If services end because the beneficiary **loses NC Medicaid eligibility**, or
- if **no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** for any reason, including hospitalization,

then **the prior approval process must be started again** under Sections 5.1 and 5.2.  
Citation: **3G-1, § 5.2.4.1** in [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment).

## If NC Medicaid terminates PDN instead of the provider

When **NC Medicaid** terminates PDN because eligibility, policy criteria, or medical necessity are not met, the policy says **NC Medicaid or its designee must provide written notice of an adverse decision to the beneficiary/legal representative, including appeal rights**.  
Citation: **3G-1, § 5.2.4.1** in [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment).

If the beneficiary is in **managed care**, federal rules require written, timely, and adequate notice of an adverse benefit determination, including:
- the action taken,
- the reasons,
- appeal rights,
- procedures for appeal,
- expedited appeal information, and
- continuation-of-benefits information.  
Citations: **42 CFR 438.404** and **42 CFR 438.10** in [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438).

## Bottom line

For a **provider-initiated PDN termination**, the clearest NC Medicaid requirement is:

- **notify NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, and
- submit the **DMA-3513 PDN Discharge Summary Form**,
- plus any extra required information depending on the reason for discharge.

If you want, I can also give you a **one-paragraph advocacy summary** distinguishing:
1. provider discharge,  
2. physician-ordered termination, and  
3. Medicaid adverse action with appeal rights.

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner orders and plan-of-care rules. Those services include:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis,
- **Home health aide services**,
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in normal life settings, and
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology/audiology services** as an optional home health service category.  
Cited in [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(b).

## Core federal conditions

For home health services under § 440.70:

- Services must be provided **on written orders** by a **physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant**, working in accordance with state law, for the services described in § 440.70(b)(1), (2), and (4).
- Those services must be part of a **written plan of care** that the ordering practitioner **reviews every 60 days**.
- For **medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** under § 440.70(b)(3), services/items must be ordered under the separate ordering and plan-of-care standards in § 440.70(a)(3), and the beneficiary’s need must be reviewed at least **annually**, with further review on a case-by-case basis.  
Cited in [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(a), (b)(3).

## Where they must be provided

Federal law says home health services must be provided **at the beneficiary’s place of residence**. But the regulation also makes clear that “place of residence” is **not limited to a private home**.

A beneficiary’s place of residence **does not include**:

- a **hospital**,
- a **nursing facility**, or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**,

with a narrow exception for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is not required to provide.  
Cited in [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c).

Federal law further states that nothing in the section should be read to prohibit home health services in **“any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** other than:

- a hospital,
- a nursing facility,
- an ICF/IID, or
- **any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board**.

It also expressly says **home health services cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**.  
Cited in [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1).

## Bottom line

Federal Medicaid law defines home health services as specified nursing, aide, medical supply/equipment/appliance, and certain therapy services furnished under the ordering and plan-of-care requirements in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70**. They must be provided at the beneficiary’s **place of residence**, meaning a setting where **normal life activities take place**, but **not** a hospital, nursing facility, ICF/IID (subject to a narrow exception), or another setting paid as inpatient room-and-board care under Medicaid. Current authority: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70.

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice eligibility, **“terminally ill” means the beneficiary has a life expectancy of six months or less**. The hospice certification/recertification materials must support that prognosis with individualized clinical information, and for later recertifications the narrative must explain why the face-to-face clinical findings support **a life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), section D, “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within two calendar days after a benefit period begins, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those two calendar days, and the **written certification still must be obtained before billing**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), § 5.4.1.

### Who must sign it
- **Initial 90-day period:** certification must come from:
  - the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; and
  - the beneficiary’s **attending physician**, if the beneficiary has one.  
  [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), § 5.4.3.

- **Subsequent benefit periods:** only the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice IDG** must certify.  
  [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), § 5.4.3.

### What the certification must contain
The certification or recertification must:
- include a **physician narrative** briefly synthesizing the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis;
- include the physician’s attestation that the narrative was composed after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- reflect the beneficiary’s **individual clinical circumstances**;
- include the **election period dates** it applies to; and
- be **signed and dated** by the certifying or recertifying physician.  
[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), section D, “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

### Timing rules
- Initial certifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the effective date of election.
- Recertifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the start of the next benefit period.  
[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), § 5.4.1; section D, “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

### Face-to-face requirement for later recertifications
Before the **third benefit period recertification and every recertification after that**, a hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner must have a **face-to-face encounter** with the beneficiary, occurring **no more than 30 calendar days before** that recertification, to gather clinical findings supporting continued hospice eligibility.  
[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), § 5.4.1.

per_question.question: What ambulance services are NOT covered by NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid does **not** cover certain ambulance services, even under the Ambulance Services policy.

## Not-covered ambulance services
Under **Section 4.2.1.4**, NC Medicaid does **not** cover:

- an ambulance call where **no treatment is needed**
- a **false alarm** ambulance response
- situations where **the beneficiary refuses all medical services**
- ambulance transport for a **medical service that is not itself covered by Medicaid**
- **commercial airline tickets**
- **airstrip fees**
- **taxes** charged separately
- **separate additional charges for nursing personnel** who are employees of a facility or ambulance service
- **waiting fees**
- separate reimbursement for **oxygen and other items/supplies**, because those are included in the base rate
- **services other than those listed in Section 3.2**  
Cite: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023.

## Other ambulance-related limits that are not covered
Under **Section 4.2.1**, NC Medicaid also does not reimburse:

- **loaded mileage to a facility that is not the nearest appropriate facility**
- transport based on a physician’s staff privileges rather than medical appropriateness
- transport based on the beneficiary’s preference for a different facility  
Cite: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) § 4.2.1, effective 12/15/2023.

## General exclusions
Separately, under **Section 4.1**, ambulance services are not covered if:

- the beneficiary does not meet the **eligibility requirements** in Section 2.0
- the beneficiary does not meet the **coverage criteria** in Section 3.0
- the service **duplicates another provider’s service**
- the service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows some speech-language evaluation and treatment services to be provided by telehealth, but only under specific conditions.

## When speech therapy can be provided by telehealth

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A**, a select set of speech and language evaluation and treatment interventions may be delivered by telehealth. Telehealth may be **medically necessary** when:

- the beneficiary’s medical condition is such that **exposure to others should be avoided**, or
- the beneficiary is in a **remote or underserved location** where access to appropriately qualified providers is limited.  
  [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (effective Feb. 1, 2025), section **e. Telehealth**

## Required limits on telehealth use

The policy also says telehealth must meet these beneficiary-specific conditions:

- **It must be an adjunct to in-person care, not a replacement**, unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable.
- **It must be in the beneficiary’s best interest**, not for the therapist’s convenience.
- **It cannot be used solely to increase therapist productivity.**  
  [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (effective Feb. 1, 2025), section **e. Telehealth**

## Ordinary speech-therapy rules still apply

Telehealth does not remove the usual medical-necessity requirements for speech-language therapy. The service still has to satisfy the underlying **speech-language therapy** criteria in Policy 10A, including applicable documentation and service-specific standards.  
[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (effective Feb. 1, 2025), section **3.2.1.3 Speech-Language Therapy (ST)**

## Bottom line

Speech therapy may be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid **only when telehealth is medically necessary and appropriate for the beneficiary**, remains generally **supplemental to in-person care**, and is **not used for therapist convenience or productivity**. It also must still meet the usual speech-therapy coverage criteria in Policy 10A.

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal law, Medicaid managed care organizations do **not automatically have a universal minimum MLR to “meet.”** The federal rule requires states to make each MCO/PIHP/PAHP **calculate and report** an MLR, and **if** a state chooses to impose a minimum MLR, that floor must be **at least 85%**. North Carolina implements that federal framework by requiring PHPs to calculate the federal/CMS-defined MLR and, in its contract, setting a **Department-defined minimum MLR threshold of 88% in aggregate across all contracted PHPs**, with plan-specific thresholds based on revenue mix. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438); [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

## Federal rule

### 1) What federal law requires
42 C.F.R. § 438.8 says the state must ensure through its contracts that each Medicaid managed care plan calculates and reports an MLR. It then provides that **if a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR**, that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85 percent**. So the federal floor is **85% for any state-imposed minimum**, not a standalone nationwide minimum imposed directly on every plan in every state. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 2) How the federal MLR is calculated
Under 42 C.F.R. § 438.8, the MLR is the ratio of:

- **Numerator:** incurred claims + expenditures for activities that improve health care quality + fraud prevention activities.
- **Denominator:** adjusted premium revenue, with taxes and licensing/regulatory fees handled under the rule’s denominator provisions.

The rule also allows a **credibility adjustment** for partially credible plans. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

At a high level, the federal numerator includes items like direct provider claims, unpaid claims liabilities, certain provider withholds, and specified incentive/bonus payments tied to measurable clinical or quality standards; it excludes non-claims administrative costs and requires certain deductions such as overpayment recoveries and prescription drug rebates. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 3) Federal oversight if a state sets a minimum
If a state imposes a minimum MLR, 42 C.F.R. § 438.74 requires the state to report annually to CMS, for each plan, at least:

- the numerator amount,
- the denominator amount,
- the MLR percentage,
- member months, and
- any remittances owed.

If remittances are required for failure to meet the state minimum, the state must reimburse CMS for the federal share of the remittance and submit a methodology report. The section reflects amendment authority noted as “as amended at 89 FR 41276, May 10, 2024.” [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## North Carolina implementation

North Carolina’s PHP contract tracks the federal rule in two layers.

### 1) NC requires calculation of the federal/CMS-defined MLR
The contract requires each PHP to calculate and report the **CMS-defined MLR** annually, aligned to the rating year, and defines it by reference to **42 C.F.R. § 438.8**. It states that:

- the CMS-defined numerator is incurred claims, health care quality improvement expenditures, and the lesser of fraud reduction expenditures or fraud reduction recoveries, as defined in the federal rule; and
- the CMS-defined denominator is adjusted premium revenue, meaning premium revenue minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing/regulatory fees as defined in the federal rule. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 2) NC also uses a Department-defined MLR
The contract additionally requires a **Department-defined MLR**, calculated similarly to the CMS-defined MLR but with NC-specific adjustments. The contract allows certain voluntary contributions to health-related resources to count in the numerator if they align with the Department’s Quality Strategy and meet specified conditions, and excludes certain other expenditures, including some separately reimbursed directed payments and certain related-party payments. It also removes from the denominator certain Department reimbursements for required additional directed payments, along with associated taxes and fees. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 3) NC’s minimum threshold
The NC contract states:

- “The minimum MLR threshold in aggregate across all contracted PHPs shall be exactly **eighty-eight percent (88%)**…”
- and says the minimum MLR threshold for an individual PHP is calculated based on the PHP’s **capitation revenue mix**, using a revenue-weighted approach across rate cells. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 4) What happens if a PHP falls below NC’s threshold
If a PHP’s **Department-defined MLR** is below the minimum threshold, the contract requires the PHP to do one of the following:

- remit a rebate to the Department,
- contribute to approved health-related resources targeted to improve outcomes and cost-effective care, or
- split the obligation between a rebate and approved contributions. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** States must require Medicaid managed care plans to **calculate and report** MLR; **if** a state sets a minimum, it must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
- **North Carolina:** NC implements that requirement in its PHP contract by requiring annual calculation of the federal/CMS-defined MLR and by imposing a **Department-defined minimum threshold of 88% in aggregate**, with plan-specific thresholds based on revenue mix and contractual rebate/contribution consequences if a PHP falls short. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

Amendment check performed for both cited sources: the knowledge base identifies [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) and the [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment) as the authoritative current documents in corpus results for this answer.

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when the beneficiary meets both the **general coverage standards** and the **CAR-T-specific standards** in Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, effective **April 1, 2025**, which appears to be the current authoritative version. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Specific coverage criteria

### 1) General Medicaid medical-necessity criteria must be met
The service must be:

- **individualized, specific, and consistent** with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and **not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**;
- able to be **safely furnished**, with **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**; and
- furnished in a manner **not primarily intended for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
  *Policy 11A-17, § 3.1* — [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

### 2) CAR-T therapy must satisfy the policy’s specific CAR-T requirements
NC Medicaid specifically requires that:

- the **CAR-T therapy has received FDA approval**;
- it is administered **according to FDA-approved guidelines** for:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions; and
- it is administered at a **certified or authorized treatment center**. If the therapy is subject to a **REMS** program, the treatment center must be **enrolled in the REMS**, and providers must be **trained to manage cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurologic toxicities**.  
  *Policy 11A-17, § 3.2.1* — [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## When NC Medicaid says CAR-T is not covered
The same policy says CAR-T is **not covered** if, among other things:

- the therapy is **not FDA-approved**;
- it is being given **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a therapy requiring **REMS** is given at a facility **not enrolled** in that REMS program;
- it is a **repeat CAR-T treatment** for someone who has already received another CAR-T therapy;
- the beneficiary’s **psychosocial history** limits ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care; or
- current beneficiary or caretaker **non-compliance** makes adherence to the required medical regimen improbable.  
  *Policy 11A-17, § 4.2.1* — [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

The policy also says coverage is not available if the beneficiary does not meet the policy’s eligibility or Section 3 criteria, if the service duplicates another provider’s service, or if it is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**.  
*Policy 11A-17, § 4.1* — [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Bottom line
In practice, NC Medicaid coverage for CAR-T cell therapy turns on these core points:

1. **Medical necessity under the general Medicaid standard**  
2. **FDA-approved CAR-T product**  
3. **Use exactly within FDA-approved parameters**  
4. **Administration at a certified/authorized center**  
5. **REMS compliance and trained providers when REMS applies**  
6. **No disqualifying issues such as repeat CAR-T, noncompliance, or noncovered/experimental use**

If you want, I can also pull out the **prior authorization documentation requirements** for CAR-T under the same policy.

per_question.question: Until what age should physicians provide fluoride varnish applications for Medicaid beneficiaries, and what oral screening requirements apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
Physicians should provide fluoride varnish **from tooth eruption until the beneficiary is 3½ years old**. NC Medicaid’s physician fluoride varnish policy requires the following oral screening components:

- **Early caries screening** and detection of notable findings in the oral cavity, including obvious pathology of hard and soft tissues, **using a dental mirror and directed light**.
- **Counseling and educational materials** on good oral hygiene practices and nutrition for children.
- **Prescribing a fluoride supplement, if indicated**, following American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines.
- **Application of fluoride varnish to all erupted primary teeth**, beginning at tooth eruption until age **3½**. [Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

## Required documentation in the health record

The beneficiary’s health record must document all of the following:

- **An oral evaluation** and any notable findings;
- **Preventive oral health and dietary counseling** with the primary caregiver;
- **Application of fluoride varnish**; and
- **Referral to a dentist, if appropriate**. [Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

## Billing limit tied to age

For the fluoride varnish procedure code **D1206**:

- it must be billed with **D0145**,
- is limited to beneficiaries **under 3½ years of age**,
- is allowed **once every 60 calendar days**, and
- is limited to **six total applications before the beneficiary reaches 3½ years of age**. [Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than the person’s individual base budget if the participant believes their needs cannot be met within that budget. Under the policy, the SIS results and the base budget are “guidelines” and “do not constitute a binding limit” on what may be requested or authorized. If the LME/MCO determines the services are medically necessary, they must be authorized even if they exceed the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective Nov. 1, 2016; amendments check returned 8-P as the authoritative current document).

## What happens if they believe the budget is not enough?

The policy says the participant:

- **may request services above the base budget** if they believe their needs cannot be met within it;
- must be told that the **base budget is not an absolute cap** on medically necessary services;
- must receive notice of **the reasons for any denial** of a service authorization request and **how to appeal**; and
- must be told **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## If very high levels of service are requested

For at least some service requests under NC Innovations, the policy provides:

- up to **12 hours daily** may be authorized for the full plan year;
- up to **16 hours daily** may be authorized for a six-month timeframe within the plan year; and
- **more than 16 hours daily** may be authorized for up to **90 days** within the plan year.

If authorization beyond that initial 90-day period is needed, the PIHP must decide based on **medical necessity**. The treatment team should then review the person’s status and identify sustainable supports, including options **within** the Innovations Waiver and **outside** it, such as Medicaid State Plan services, with that information included in the ISP. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

An NC Innovations base budget is **not a hard ceiling**. If a participant’s needs cannot be met within that amount, they can ask for more services, and medically necessary services can be authorized above the budget. If the request is denied, the participant must be told why and how to **appeal**, and they may also file a **grievance** about the base budget.
